korean-sheet-masks-wholesale.title: Korean Sheet Masks: How a Buyer Builds a Shelf
korean-sheet-masks-wholesale.excerpt: Sheet masks are the most accessible entry point into Korean cosmetics. Using the LEBELAGE line as an example, we look at how a buyer can turn dozens of SKUs into a coherent assortment rather than a random grab-bag.
korean-sheet-masks-wholesale.seoTitle: Korean Sheet Masks for Buyers · Teranova
korean-sheet-masks-wholesale.seoDesc: A buyer's guide to Korean sheet masks: the logic behind the LEBELAGE line, key actives, packaging formats, and what to check before you place an order.

p: A sheet mask is one of the most recognizable K-beauty products and, at the same time, one of the easiest categories to start buying into: a low per-unit price, simple usage mechanics, and broad ingredient coverage. A good example of how this category works from the inside is the MASK PACK line from LEBELAGE, produced by the Korean company DONGDONGGURIMOO CO., LTD. The company's second brand, HEEYUL, specializes in hair care, but sheet masks are one of LEBELAGE's largest product categories in their own right: the brand's current price list counts 42 items out of 355 across 30 categories.

sections.h: Why sheet masks are the entry point into the category
p: For a buyer stepping into Korean cosmetics for the first time, sheet masks remove several risks at once. The entry price is low, which lets you test demand without committing heavily to a single item. The format invites impulse purchases: a mask is easy to add to the cart "just to try" alongside a core skincare routine. It also works well as a gift or seasonal item — sets pack neatly for holidays or "beauty box" bundles.

Another advantage is marketplace compatibility: a sheet mask is compact, needs no special storage conditions, and fits neatly into a product listing with a promise the customer immediately understands — soothe, hydrate, refresh. That's exactly why the category often becomes a buyer's first purchase in Korean cosmetics, before they move on to more complex products like serums, creams, or full care programs.

sections.h: Building an assortment, not a random set of SKUs
p: The most common mistake in a first order is picking masks by the look of the packaging or an arbitrary mix of items. What actually works is building the line around a skin concern, not a SKU list. In LEBELAGE's assortment this shows up in the logic of the actives: centella (Cica) and panthenol for soothing irritated, sensitive skin; hyaluronic acid, PDRN, and snail mucin for intensive hydration and repair; vitamin C and niacinamide for brightening; collagen, peptides, retinol, and glutathione for the anti-age line; tea tree and green tea for oily and problem skin; ceramides for strengthening the barrier.

This kind of breakdown across four or five concerns — soothing, hydration, brightening, anti-aging, sebum control — gives a buyer a real basis for merchandising: the shelf can be presented to the customer not as "just masks," but as "a program for a specific skin concern," which noticeably simplifies selling, whether offline or on a marketplace.

sections.h: What to check before ordering
p: When choosing specific items, it's worth checking the base formula and the stated key active against the line's positioning; the sheet's thickness, which determines both the feel during use and how well it holds the essence; the shelf life of the batch; and the packaging format — single units or sets (LEBELAGE, for example, offers sets of 10 or 20 masks) — which shapes shelf pricing logic and convenience across different sales channels.

For markets with regulatory requirements, it's worth confirming registration status upfront — MoCRA in the US, CPNP in the EU, SCPN in the UK: some items in the line carry these registrations, but their current validity needs to be confirmed with documentation at the deal stage, not assumed from the brand's general description. As a benchmark, wholesale prices for sheet masks start at around $1 per unit (supply price, as of July 2026) — exact prices, minimum order quantities, and delivery terms are provided by Teranova on request once a deal moves into specifics. Our role in this process is to coordinate and support the deal between the buyer and the manufacturer in Korea, not to act as a party making promises about the outcome.

korean-scalp-care-category.title: Korean Scalp Care: A New Category for Buyers, Featuring HEEYUL
korean-scalp-care-category.excerpt: Korean scalp care grows out of facial skincare logic and applies it to the scalp — with a higher price point and more regular consumption. We break down the category using the HEEYUL brand from DONGDONGGURIMOO.
korean-scalp-care-category.seoTitle: Korean Scalp Care for Buyers · Teranova
korean-scalp-care-category.seoDesc: Korean scalp care as a category for importers: routine logic, formulas, and what to check before ordering — featuring the HEEYUL brand from DONGDONGGURIMOO.

p: Korean beauty has long trained the market to expect multi-step facial skincare — and that same logic is now moving to the scalp. For a buyer looking for a category with a clear demand structure rather than a one-off hit, this is a signal worth noticing: scalp care behaves less like ordinary shampoo and more like skincare — with formulas, actives, and an application routine. Let's look at what this category consists of and how Korean manufacturers structure it, using the HEEYUL brand from the South Korean company DONGDONGGURIMOO CO., LTD as an example.

sections.h: Why scalp care is a growing category
p: The logic is simple: if facial skin needs cleansing, hydration, and targeted actives, the scalp is built similarly and deserves the same attention. Korean brands were among the first to bring facial-care approaches to the scalp — serum textures, concentrated ampoules, course-based use. For a buyer this means a higher average ticket than a regular shampoo and, more importantly, regular repeat consumption: products in this category are bought as a course rather than a one-off, which drives repeat orders.

Another advantage is the formula itself. Scalp care formulas often feature actives a buyer already recognizes from facial skincare: panthenol, ceramides, peptides, centella asiatica, keratin for hair structure. This makes it easier to position the products on the shelf next to skincare, not just in the shampoo aisle.

sections.h: How the routine works — and why it sells well as a set
p: A typical Korean scalp care routine has three steps: cleansing (shampoo), care (conditioner or mask), and a cosmetic-treatment step — a tonic or a targeted ampoule. This structure is convenient not only for the consumer but for the buyer as well: three products naturally combine into a starter set, which lowers the barrier for the end customer and raises the average ticket per sale.

HEEYUL, for example, has an anti-hair-loss category line built exactly on this set of steps — shampoo, conditioner, tonic, and ampoule — along with separate kits inspired by Korean herbal medicine (hanbang). It's important to phrase the positioning precisely: these are scalp-care and scalp-health-support products, not treatments for hair loss or alopecia — this is cosmetics, not medicine.

sections.h: HEEYUL and DONGDONGGURIMOO: what's behind the brand
p: HEEYUL is the dedicated hair-care brand of the Korean company DONGDONGGURIMOO CO., LTD; the company's second brand, LEBELAGE, covers facial skincare and color cosmetics. This kind of split is typical for full-cycle Korean manufacturers: one company, different brands for different categories, which makes it easier for a buyer to negotiate assortment across several directions at once.

In the company's price list, the HAIR CARE category counts 12 items out of 355 products across 30 catalog categories — meaning hair care isn't the main segment, but it is a distinct and reasonably detailed one that can be bought into selectively, without taking on the whole catalog.

sections.h: What to check before ordering
p: Before adding scalp care to an order, a buyer should go through several points: package size and format (retail size, travel formats, ampoule volume), the stated formula and how well it matches the target market's expectations, the product's target audience (general care or anti-hair-loss category), the registrations and documents required to import into a specific jurisdiction, and whether a ready-made starter set exists — this speeds up launch and lowers risk for a distributor entering the category for the first time.

Exact wholesale terms, prices, and delivery basis for HEEYUL and other items in the DONGDONGGURIMOO catalog are discussed individually at the deal stage. Teranova coordinates and supports these negotiations with the Korean side, taking the operational part off the buyer's plate — from clarifying the formula to logistics.

korean-makeup-suncare-wholesale.title: Korean Makeup and Suncare Wholesale: Building a Starter Assortment
korean-makeup-suncare-wholesale.excerpt: Using the LEBELAGE brand as an example, we break down how a buyer builds a first wholesale order of Korean color cosmetics and SPF products — from assortment logic to the questions that need answers before ordering.
korean-makeup-suncare-wholesale.seoDesc: How to build a starter wholesale order of Korean makeup and suncare: category logic, LEBELAGE price-list scale, and what to confirm before you order.

p: When a buyer puts together a first order of Korean cosmetics, the most common mistake is trying to take "everything at once": dozens of SKUs across different categories with no sense of which ones will sell themselves and which will just sit in the warehouse. Let's look at a working approach to building a starter assortment, using the current LEBELAGE price list (manufacturer: the Korean company DONGDONGGURIMOO CO., LTD.), where color cosmetics and suncare sit alongside skincare in a single catalog of 355 items across 30 categories.

sections.h: What's in the category, and how much of it
p: In the LEBELAGE price list, color cosmetics (MAKE-UP) account for 47 items: lip and cheek tints, lipsticks, mascaras, cushions, brow pencils — the whole basic set for a mass-market or pharmacy-format shelf. Suncare (SUN CARE) is a separate line of 21 items, including compact formats (sticks, tubes around 40 ml) and water-resistant versions suited to travel and resort displays.

For scale, by comparison: creams — 39 items, facial cleansers — 32, ampoules — 25, toners — 22. It's worth keeping this in mind, because makeup and SPF in this line aren't the only strong block, but one of several, and it makes sense to combine them with skincare items in a single shipment rather than order them in isolation.

sections.h: Why suncare is a strong anchor category
p: Sun protection products from Korea are one of the most stable K-beauty segments on international markets, and there's a clear reason for it: seasonality here is flatter than it first appears. Compact SPF formats are used not just in summer but as part of a daily routine, which gives more even demand throughout the year and a high repeat-purchase frequency — meaning a predictable reorder for the buyer.

On top of that, suncare has a request that's easy to explain to the end customer: SPF factor, water resistance, a light texture — there's no need to explain "why this." That's why, in a starter assortment, it makes sense to place the SPF line among the anchor items alongside tints and cushions, rather than treat it as a secondary add-on to makeup.

sections.h: How to structure a starter order: three layers of assortment
p: A working model is three layers. Anchor items — suncare, lip and cheek tints, cushions — are what drives core turnover and shelf recognition for the line. Supporting items — basic skincare (creams, facial cleansers, toners) — extend the ticket and drive repeat customer visits. Impulse items — masks and targeted novelties — are added at the end of the build to refresh the display, but shouldn't take up the main budget of a first order.

Before finalizing an order, a few questions with the supplier are worth closing: how many shades to stock in the tint and cushion color range for the target audience, the shelf life of the batch at time of shipment, the labeling requirements in force in the target market, and the carton multiple — that is, the minimum order step for each item. These are standard questions that remove most of the risk at the negotiation stage, before shipment.

On registrations specifically: in the current LEBELAGE price list, a MoCRA (US) registration mark appears on 240 items, EU CPNP on 77, UK SCPN on 76. An important caveat: having a registration or listing in these systems isn't a regulator's approval of the product — it's a filing procedure, not a safety or efficacy certificate. The current validity and scope of registration for specific SKUs need to be confirmed at the deal stage, not taken from the price list as a final status.

On wholesale pricing: a benchmark for mass makeup and SPF categories is around $1.5–3 per item (Supply Price, July 2026 data), but exact prices and terms for a specific batch are available on request. In these deals, Teranova coordinates and supports the process between buyer and supplier — from clarifying the assortment to agreeing terms — without taking on obligations for sales outcomes or regulatory status.

wnt-cxxc5-scalp-science.title: Wnt Signaling and CXXC5: The Science Behind WNT ON Technology
wnt-cxxc5-scalp-science.excerpt: We break down the scientific basis of WNT ON technology from the Korean brand DermaRegeon: what the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is, where the CXXC5 protein fits in — and why a B2B buyer needs to keep a component's mechanism separate from a finished product's proven efficacy.
wnt-cxxc5-scalp-science.seoTitle: Wnt Signaling and CXXC5: Science Behind WNT ON · Teranova
wnt-cxxc5-scalp-science.seoDesc: WNT ON technology from DermaRegeon: the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, the role of CXXC5, preclinical data on KY19382 and PTD-DBM, and what a buyer can and can't claim.

p: Korean biotech companies increasingly enter cosmetics not with a formula, but with a scientific platform originally built for entirely different purposes. CK Regeon is a clear example: the company was founded in 2016 in Korea, based at Yonsei Engineering Research Park, and its CEO is Professor Kang-Yell Choi, who has studied the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway for many years. In 2025, the company's research gave rise to the cosmetic brand portfolio DermaRegeon, with the HAIRREGEON line (professional care) and the HERIBON line (home care), united under a technology called WNT ON. For a buyer who has to present this story to their own market, it's important to understand what's actually behind this name — and exactly where the line between science and marketing runs.

sections.h: What the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is — in plain terms
p: Wnt/β-catenin is one of the cell's fundamental signaling pathways, studied in developmental and regenerative biology for decades. In simple terms, it's an intracellular "communication system" that tells cells when to divide, differentiate, and form tissue. It's involved in embryonic development, wound healing, and the renewal of tissues with a high rate of cell turnover — which includes the hair follicle, which cycles through growth, rest, and renewal throughout life.

That's exactly why the Wnt pathway has been a focus of fundamental skin and hair science for decades — not as a marketing term, but as the subject of serious laboratory research in dermatology and developmental biology.

sections.h: CXXC5 and the logic of "releasing the brake"
p: In this context, researchers describe the CXXC5 protein as a negative regulator of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway — essentially one of the system's natural "brakes." The logic behind WNT ON technology isn't to "switch on" the pathway directly, but to modulate it by interacting with CXXC5, easing off that braking mechanism. This is described in two preclinical papers: Lee and colleagues (Journal of Investigative Dermatology, 2017) studied the PTD-DBM peptide, which targets CXXC5; Ryu and colleagues (British Journal of Pharmacology, 2021) studied KY19382, a small molecule with a similar mechanism of action. The cosmetic formulas under WNT ON list KY19382 and hesperidin as components.

Precision of wording matters here: both publications are preclinical studies, carried out in cell cultures, ex vivo tissue cultures, and animal models. No published human clinical studies on these formulations are publicly available. That doesn't make the mechanism any less interesting to skin science — but it does mean we're talking about a component's studied molecular mechanism, not the proven clinical efficacy of a finished cosmetic product.

sections.h: Where the line runs between mechanism and product claim
p: For a B2B distributor, this line isn't a theoretical nuance — it's a direct regulatory risk. Wording like "stops hair loss," "cures baldness," or "clinically proven efficacy" falls into the category of therapeutic claims and, in most jurisdictions, requires an entirely different level of evidence and registration than cosmetic products. DermaRegeon's products are scalp and hair care products, and the correct way to talk about them is in exactly these terms: a formula built on a studied scientific mechanism, not a therapeutic effect confirmed by human clinical trials.

The difference between "we use a component whose mechanism has been studied in peer-reviewed scientific journals" and "we have clinically proven the product's efficacy" is the difference between a strong, honest scientific brand story and a potential regulatory violation on a pharmacy or marketplace shelf. A buyer adapting communication for their own market should stick to the first framing and avoid the second — regardless of how the brand's original marketing sounds.

sections.h: What this gives the buyer
p: The practical takeaway for a wholesale buyer: DermaRegeon has something rare for a cosmetics category — a formula logic traceable back to peer-reviewed publications, rather than an abstract "innovative complex." That's a strong argument for shelf positioning and for a distributor presentation, provided the communication is built carefully and doesn't cross into therapeutic promises. Teranova coordinates and supports deals with Korean manufacturers, including reviewing scientific and regulatory wording before entering a local market; exact supply terms and wholesale prices for the HAIRREGEON and HERIBON lines are available on request.

heribon-four-step-routine.title: HERIBON: A Four-Step Scalp Care Routine from CK Regeon
heribon-four-step-routine.excerpt: We break down the structure of the HERIBON home line from CK Regeon — from the logic of its four-step routine to the wholesale economics for a distributor.
heribon-four-step-routine.seoDesc: HERIBON from CK Regeon: a four-step scalp care routine, wholesale prices, and minimum order quantities. How a distributor can launch the line through Teranova.

p: In 2025, the Korean biotech company CK Regeon launched a two-brand scalp-care portfolio: the professional HAIRREGEON line for salons and the home-use HERIBON line for retail customers. HERIBON is built around a single four-step routine under the overall name "WNT ON" — and it's exactly this structure that makes the line an easy entry point for a distributor looking for a ready-made shelf rather than a single SKU.

sections.h: The logic of the four-step routine
p: The order of steps in WNT ON mirrors the facial-care logic customers already know, applied to the scalp: first, cleansing with shampoo (500 ml), then deeper exfoliation with a scalp scaler (300 ml), followed by length care with a mask (250 ml), and finally a scalp tonic (50 ml) as the closing step of the routine. This sequence reads instantly to the customer and needs no explanation on the shelf: shampoo is the base, the scaler is for once or twice a week for deeper cleansing, the mask cares for the hair length, and the tonic is a light finishing touch.

For a distributor, this means the line can be sold as a system rather than a set of unrelated items. At the core of the technology is the WNT ON complex with KY19382 and hesperidin as components, which gives all four products a single narrative and simplifies working on shelf copy and marketplace listings.

sections.h: Economics for the distributor
p: Wholesale prices across the line follow a clear spread: the shampoo is around $11, the scaler and mask are $9.75 each, and the tonic is $7.50. Recommended retail is roughly double the wholesale price for each item ($22, $19.5, $19.5, and $15 respectively), giving a standard, predictable margin for the retail channel without needing to explain unusual pricing to the customer.

Within the line, items play different roles. The tonic is the most accessible entry point on price, but requires an order of at least 100 units: that makes it a convenient consumable for salon kits, samples, and promotional mechanics, rather than a standalone margin driver. The shampoo, with a minimum order of 20 units and the highest wholesale price, is the natural anchor of the category, around which the display is built. The scaler and mask, with a minimum order of 25 units, sit in between and are typically bought as an upsell alongside the shampoo.

sections.h: How to bring in the line
p: Supply terms are EXW/FOB Korea for orders from $10,000, so it makes sense to plan not for a single SKU but for the full set of four items, accounting for the minimum order quantity on each. A starter set of all four steps gives a full shelf story and lets the line be sold as a system; a test order of a single anchor product (the shampoo) works if the channel is new and you first need to gauge turnover before bringing in the other three items.

By sales channel, the line fits well into pharmacy and specialized hair-care chains, beauty salons (as a retail extension of the professional HAIRREGEON line), and marketplaces, where the "4-step set" format works as a standalone listing. Before placing an order, Teranova coordinates and supports clarification of three points: labeling and registration requirements for the target market, current production lead times, and logistics from Korea to the destination.

professional-scalp-boosters.title: Two-Component Scalp Boosters: The HAIRREGEON Format
professional-scalp-boosters.excerpt: We break down the "powder plus solvent" format using the professional HAIRREGEON line from the Korean biotech company CK Regeon as an example — and what a buyer needs to understand about this segment before ordering.
professional-scalp-boosters.seoDesc: The powder-plus-solvent format in professional scalp care, using HAIRREGEON (CK Regeon) as an example: economics, MOQ, and who to sell to. A guide from Teranova.

p: Korea's professional scalp-care segment is increasingly offering buyers not a ready-made serum, but a two-component system mixed right before use in the salon. One notable example of this format is the HAIRREGEON line, developed by the biotech company CK Regeon (the parent company behind the DermaRegeon brand, also known for its home-use HERIBON line). Below is a look at why the industry favors this way of delivering an active ingredient, and what it means for a wholesale order.

sections.h: Why separate the active ingredient from the solvent
p: The line's flagship product, the PTD-DBM Hair Booster set, consists of two vials: Vial 1 contains a lyophilized (freeze-dried) powder of the active ingredient weighing 200 mg, and Vial 2 is a 5 ml solvent. One set is designed for a single use or for use over a course of treatment, and the package contains 5 such sets.

Lyophilization is a standard technique in the cosmetics and pharmaceutical industry for unstable active ingredients: in dry form, the substance is less prone to oxidation and degradation during storage and transport, and shelf life increases many times over compared to a ready-mixed water solution. Mixing the powder with the solvent right before applying it to the scalp gives the specialist confidence that the client is getting a freshly prepared formula, not a solution that may have lost activity over weeks or months in storage or on a shelf. This is a standard approach for any serum with unstable peptide or bioactive components — the two-component format by itself isn't a medical characteristic, it's an engineering solution for formula stability.

sections.h: What's known about the active ingredient — and where the line is drawn
p: The active ingredient in the powder, PTD-DBM, is a peptide whose mechanism of action at the preclinical level (in vitro and in animal models) is described in Lee et al., published in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology in 2017: the authors describe competitive binding to the CXXC5 protein. This is cell- and animal-level research, not data from human clinical trials, and it's important for a buyer to communicate this distinction to distributors and salons in the target market — both in marketing materials and in instructions for the end specialist.

HAIRREGEON and products based on PTD-DBM are positioned by the manufacturer as cosmetic products for external scalp care within professional salon programs. Wording about treating alopecia, stopping hair loss, or clinically proven efficacy, along with any references to injectable, mesotherapy, or other intradermal use (including MTS protocols), doesn't match the product's status and shouldn't be used in promotion — this applies both to Teranova itself and to partners we help enter this market.

sections.h: Economics of the professional segment for a buyer
p: The wholesale price is roughly $160 per package (5 sets) on FCA terms, with a minimum order of 5 packages. For the professional B2B segment, this is a fairly comfortable entry threshold: it allows testing the product in a local market without large inventory commitments, before scaling up an order for a salon network or distribution network.

The sales model in this segment differs fundamentally from mass market: the product isn't meant for a retail shelf but is sold through salons, trichology studios, and aesthetic clinics, where it's used over a course under a specialist's supervision. The high per-package price is offset by the fact that the end service at the salon generates its own margin for the partner, rather than competing on price with home care. Candidates for this order are professional beauty-industry distributors, trichology clinic chains, and salons with a scalp-therapy focus that already work with professional, not mass-market, cosmetics.

sections.h: What to confirm before ordering
p: Before bringing the product into a specific market, it's worth closing a few practical questions: the regulatory status of the cosmetic product in the destination country (in some countries, professional scalp cosmetics are registered differently from mass retail), labeling and instruction-translation requirements, storage conditions for the lyophilized powder and the mixed solution, and whether salon staff need training on the application protocol. Teranova coordinates and supports this part of the work — from requesting current terms and batch details from the Korean side to arranging logistics and checking that documentation matches the target market's requirements — leaving final commercial and regulatory decisions to the partner.
